Challenge 21: Our Age Verification and Responsible Retailing Policy

Drinks House 247 is a licensed alcohol retailer delivering across London 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Selling alcohol is a privilege granted under licence, and we take the responsibilities that come with it seriously. Every single delivery we make is subject to our Challenge 21 policy.

What Challenge 21 means

The legal minimum age to purchase alcohol in the United Kingdom is 18. Challenge 21 goes further: if the person receiving a delivery appears to be under 21, our driver will ask to see photo identification before handing anything over. Looking under 21 is not an accusation — it is simply the trigger for a check. Plenty of customers well over 18 are asked for ID, and that is exactly how the policy is meant to work.

Why we operate it

Judging age by appearance is genuinely difficult, particularly at a doorstep, at night, in poor light, and often in a hurry. Challenge 21 removes guesswork from our drivers' hands. By setting the checking threshold three years above the legal age, we build in a margin that protects young people, protects our drivers from being put in an impossible position, and protects our licence. It is a standard adopted across responsible UK retail and it is applied here without exception.

We also work with the police in the areas we serve. Where we have reason to believe someone under 18 has attempted to buy alcohol, we may pass on a description and the contact and address details supplied with the order.

ID we accept

Please have one of the following ready when your delivery arrives:

  • A valid passport (UK or international)
  • A UK photocard driving licence (full or provisional)
  • A PASS-accredited proof of age card, carrying the PASS hologram — for example a Citizencard or Validate card

Whichever you use, it must be the original document, in date, undamaged, and clearly showing your photograph and date of birth. We cannot accept photocopies, scans, screenshots, photographs of ID on a phone, student cards, travel cards or bank cards. Our driver may briefly examine the document; they will not retain it or record it beyond confirming the check took place.

If ID cannot be produced

If you appear to be under 21 and cannot produce an acceptable form of ID, our driver will refuse to complete the delivery and will return the alcohol to us. Our drivers have no discretion in this and are instructed not to negotiate. Please do not ask them to make an exception — they are following a policy designed to protect them.

Where a delivery is refused for this reason, the goods will be returned and your order will be dealt with by our customer service team. Any delivery charge already incurred may not be refundable in these circumstances. If a delivery to you has been refused, please call us on 0203 488 3266 or email sales@drinkshouse247.co.uk so we can look at your order.

Proxy purchase — buying for under-18s

It is a criminal offence in the UK to buy or attempt to buy alcohol on behalf of a person under 18. This is known as proxy purchasing. It applies even where the person placing and paying for the order is comfortably over 18.

If our driver has reasonable grounds to believe that alcohol is being bought for someone under 18 — for example, where under-18s are present and are clearly the intended recipients — the delivery will be refused, regardless of the age of the person who answers the door. Please do not put our drivers in that position.

Refusing service to intoxicated persons

It is also an offence to sell alcohol to a person who is drunk. Where our driver considers that the person receiving the order is intoxicated, they may refuse to hand over the delivery. As with age checks, this is a judgement our drivers are entitled and expected to make, and it is not open to negotiation at the door. Our drivers may likewise decline to complete a delivery where they feel unsafe or are subjected to abuse.

Helping your delivery go smoothly

  • Have your ID out and ready before the driver arrives — it saves everyone time.
  • The person named on the order should ideally be the person who answers the door.
  • Make sure your delivery address, entry instructions and phone number are accurate at checkout.
  • If you are ordering as a gift for someone else, make sure the recipient is over 18 and knows to expect a delivery requiring ID.

What is Champagne? The Basics

Champagne is distinguished from other sparkling wines by two things: its geographic origin and its production method — the méthode champenoise (traditional method). This involves a primary fermentation followed by a crucial secondary fermentation in the bottle, which creates the signature bubbles. The Champagne region’s cool climate and chalky soil are ideal for the three main grape varieties:

  • Chardonnay — adds elegance, freshness, and citrus notes
  • Pinot Noir — adds body, structure, and red fruit character
  • Pinot Meunier — adds roundness and approachability

Types of Champagne

  • Non-Vintage (NV) — blends wines from multiple years for a consistent house style; accounts for the majority of production
  • Vintage — made entirely from one exceptional harvest year; only produced in the best years
  • Blanc de Blancs — made solely from Chardonnay; crisp, elegant, and mineral-driven
  • Blanc de Noirs — made from Pinot Noir and/or Pinot Meunier; full-bodied and structured
  • Rosé Champagne — made by blending a small amount of red wine; vibrant red berry notes
  • Prestige Cuvée — the finest expression of a house; examples include Dom Pérignon and Krug Grande Cuvée

Champagne Sweetness Levels Explained

  • Brut Nature / Zero Dosage — bone dry, no added sugar
  • Extra Brut — very dry
  • Brut — dry; the most common style
  • Extra Sec — off-dry
  • Sec — medium dry
  • Demi-Sec — medium sweet; ideal with desserts
  • Doux — sweet; the sweetest style

How Champagne is Made

The méthode champenoise is a labour-intensive process requiring precision and skill:

  • Primary fermentation — base wine is produced from the harvest
  • Blending (assemblage) — the winemaker blends different grape varieties and reserve wines
  • Secondary fermentation — yeast and sugar (liqueur de tirage) are added; the bottle is sealed and CO₂ is trapped, creating bubbles
  • Ageing on lees — minimum 15 months for NV, 3 years for vintage; top houses often age for much longer
  • Riddling (remuage) — bottles are gradually turned to collect sediment in the neck
  • Disgorgement (dégorgement) — sediment is removed; dosage (sugar solution) is added to determine final sweetness

Experience the difference with Dom Pérignon — aged for a minimum of 8 years before release.

How to Taste Champagne

A quality champagne will show:

  • Bubbles: Fine, persistent, and rising in a steady stream
  • Colour: Pale gold to deep amber depending on age and style
  • Nose: Citrus, green apple, brioche, almond, toast, and yeast
  • Palate: Balanced acidity, complexity, and a long, clean finish

Explore fine examples including Veuve Clicquot, Moët & Chandon, and Bollinger.

How to Serve Champagne

  • Temperature: 8–10°C — chill for 2–3 hours in the fridge or 30 minutes in an ice bucket
  • Glass: Tulip-shaped glass (not a flat coupe or narrow flute) to best appreciate aromas and bubbles
  • Opening: Remove the foil and cage, hold the cork firmly, and rotate the bottle slowly — aim for a gentle sigh, not a loud pop
  • Pouring: Tilt the glass and pour slowly to preserve the bubbles

How to Store Champagne

  • Store in a cool (10–12°C), dark place away from direct sunlight and vibration
  • Keep bottles horizontal to maintain the cork seal
  • Non-vintage champagne: consume within 3–4 years of purchase
  • Vintage champagne: can last 10+ years when well stored
  • Opened bottle: use a champagne stopper and consume within 1–2 days

Champagne Food Pairings

  • Brut NV: Oysters, caviar, smoked salmon, fine seafood, sushi
  • Blanc de Blancs: Grilled lobster, scallops, goat cheese, light salads
  • Rosé Champagne: Charcuterie, strawberries, salmon, light meat dishes
  • Vintage / Prestige Cuvée: Truffle dishes, foie gras, aged cheeses, caviar
  • Demi-Sec: Fruit tarts, crème brülée, light desserts

Why Bottle Size Matters

The size of a champagne bottle influences how the champagne ages. Larger bottles often result in better ageing, allowing the champagne to develop richer and more refined flavours due to a more favourable air-to-liquid ratio. A Magnum, for example, is widely considered to produce the finest aged champagne.

Champagne Bottle Sizes Available at Drinks House 247

Mini Bottle (20cl)

Ideal for single servings, our mini bottles (piccolos) are perfect for offering a taste of luxury without opening a full-sized bottle. Great for party favours and individual gifts.

Half Bottle (37.5cl)

Standard Bottle (75cl)

The gold standard for most celebrations, providing approximately six glasses. Ideal for intimate gatherings, family meals, or as a champagne gift.

Magnum (1.5L)

A Magnum contains the equivalent of two standard bottles and is often preferred for its superior ageing potential and impressive presence at parties and larger gatherings. Approximately 12 glasses.

Jeroboam (3L)

Holding four standard bottles (approximately 24 glasses), a Jeroboam ensures your celebration will be well-supplied. A popular choice for weddings and significant events.

Methuselah (6L)

Salmanazar (9L)

Balthazar (12L)

Equal to sixteen standard bottles (approximately 96 glasses), the Balthazar is chosen for the most extravagant events, serving as both a beverage and a statement piece.

Nebuchadnezzar (15L)

The largest standard size we offer, a Nebuchadnezzar holds twenty standard bottles (approximately 120 glasses) and is the ultimate choice for grand celebrations, providing ample champagne for over one hundred guests.

Selecting the Right Champagne Bottle Size

Champagne Styles

Brut Nature Champagne

With no added sugar (dosage), Brut Nature lets the grapes and terroir shine, delivering a tantalisingly dry and refreshing taste. The purest expression of champagne’s character.

Extra Brut Champagne

With an incredibly low dosage, Extra Brut offers a harmonious balance between crispness and a touch of richness — vibrantly zesty and luxuriously dry.

Brut Champagne

The classic champagne style. Combining a dry to slightly off-dry profile with a perfect balance of fruitiness and refreshing acidity, Brut champagne is the most versatile and widely enjoyed style.

Extra Sec Champagne

With a slightly higher dosage, Extra Sec offers a refined and nuanced experience — fruity notes dancing alongside vibrant bubbles with a subtle touch of sweetness.

Sec Champagne

With a medium level of residual sugar, Sec champagne delicately balances the region’s signature acidity with a touch of luscious sweetness.

Demi-Sec Champagne

With a higher dosage of residual sugar, Demi-Sec champagne offers a rich and opulent experience — ideal with desserts and sweet dishes.

Doux Champagne

The sweetest champagne style, Doux boasts the highest dosage of residual sugar — a rare and indulgent treat for those who love sweetness.

Champagne Ageing Categories

Non-Vintage Champagne

Crafted by blending wines from different years, Non-Vintage champagne ensures a consistent house style with every bottle. The most widely available and approachable category.

Vintage Champagne

Made from a single exceptional year, Vintage champagne captures the unique character of that specific harvest — reflecting the climate, terroir, and artistry of the winemaker. Each bottle tells a story.

Multi-Vintage Champagne (Cuvée de Prestige)

Also known as Luxury Cuvée, Multi-Vintage champagne is a harmonious blend of exceptional wines from extraordinary years combined with reserve wines. The pinnacle of champagne craftsmanship.

Champagne Regional Classifications

Grand Cru

Grand Cru champagnes come from the most prestigious villages in the Champagne region, producing grapes of unparalleled quality. Every bottle reflects exceptional finesse, complexity, and a true sense of place.

Premier Cru

Slightly below Grand Cru in classification, Premier Cru vineyards produce grapes that embody the elegance and finesse for which Champagne is renowned — offering a captivating balance between quality and value.

Autre Cru

Autre Cru vineyards contribute their own unique charm and flavours to the region’s tapestry. An excellent way to explore lesser-known terroirs and discover distinctive champagnes.

Montagne de Reims

Known for Pinot Noir, this area produces champagnes with structure and robustness. Key houses include:

  • Krug: Renowned for its rich, complex champagnes that epitomize luxury.
  • Taittinger: Known for its finesse, often using a higher proportion of Chardonnay.
  • Pommery: Created the first Brut champagne, catering to British preferences for drier styles.
  • Charles Heidsieck: Esteemed for its sophisticated champagnes enriched with significant reserve wines.

Côte des Blancs

  • Pol Roger: Preferred by British aristocracy, known for its balanced and elegant champagnes.
  • Pierre Peters: A respected grower-producer celebrated for its pure Chardonnay champagnes.

Vallée de la Marne

This subregion is recognized for Pinot Meunier, adding richness and approachability to the champagnes.

  • Billecart-Salmon: Particularly famous for its refined Rosé and balanced blends.
  • Mercier: Targets a broad audience with its accessible and easy-drinking champagnes.
  • Nicolas Feuillatte: One of the largest producers, known for its expressive range.

Côte des Bar

Celebrated for its unique Pinot Noir, this subregion produces distinctively bold champagnes.

  • Drappier: Known for its minimal sulfur use and a high proportion of Pinot Noir.
  • Jacques Selosse: Innovator producing single-vineyard champagnes with a cult following.

Additional Noteworthy Brands Across the Region

  • Perrier-Jouët: Famous for its floral and intricate champagnes, particularly the Belle Epoque series.

  • Laurent-Perrier: Known for its fresh and elegant style, including the widely acclaimed Laurent-Perrier Cuvée Rosé.
  • Philipponnat: Offers a range of champagnes but is best known for the Clos des Goisses.
  • Armand de Brignac (Ace of Spades): Ultra-premium brand known for its striking bottles and celebrity appeal.

Understanding Champagne Types

Each champagne style offers a unique tasting experience and pairs differently with food:

Sec

Moderately sweet, Sec champagne adapts to a variety of dishes — especially those with a hint of sweetness.

Demi-Sec

Sweeter than Sec, Demi-Sec champagne is an indulgent accompaniment to desserts and dishes with a sweet profile.

Extra Brut

Bone-dry and invigorating, Extra Brut champagne is a crisp companion for light, delicate dishes.

Doux

The sweetest champagne style, Doux pairs beautifully with rich, sweet desserts.

Zero Dosage

With no added sugar, Zero Dosage is the driest champagne. It shines alongside dishes with high acidity or salt content.

Food Pairings for Zero Dosage Champagne

Malbec vs Merlot: Overview

Malbec

Malbec is a purple grape variety originating in France but now primarily associated with Argentina, where it is considered the national variety. Argentine Malbecs are ripe, plush, and full-bodied with flavours of blackberry, plum, leather, and smoky oak. In its native Cahors region of France, Malbec is more rustic with firm tannins and tart currant notes — sometimes called “the black wine” for its deep, inky colour.

Merlot

Merlot is one of the primary grapes of Bordeaux and the most widely planted grape in the Bordeaux wine regions. Merlot wines are round, plump, and juicy with flavours of blackberry, cherry, plum, chocolate, and herbal notes. Its softer tannins make it one of the most approachable and versatile red wines in the world.

Key Differences: Malbec vs Merlot

  • Body: Malbec is typically full-bodied (13.5–15% ABV); Merlot is medium to full-bodied (12–14% ABV)
  • Tannins: Malbec has higher tannins; Merlot has softer, rounder tannins
  • Flavour: Malbec — dark fruit, spice, earth; Merlot — ripe red fruit, chocolate, herbs
  • Colour: Malbec is darker and inkier; Merlot is a lighter ruby red
  • Origin: Malbec — Argentina (Mendoza) and France (Cahors); Merlot — Bordeaux, California, Italy

Food Pairings

Malbec pairs best with hearty, robust foods: red meat, BBQ, spicy dishes, and strong cheeses. Merlot is more versatile — excellent with poultry, red meat, pasta, and a wide range of cheeses. Browse our red wine collection to find the perfect bottle for your meal.

Interesting Facts

  • Malbec World Day is celebrated on April 17th, commemorating the day Argentina officially began transforming its wine industry in 1853
  • The name Merlot is thought to derive from merle, the French word for blackbird — a reference to the grape’s dark colour
  • Both Malbec and Merlot share a common parent grape: Cabernet Franc
  • Merlot is the second most planted grape in the world after Cabernet Sauvignon

About Nebbiolo

Nebbiolo is the noble grape behind some of Italy’s most esteemed red wines. Named after the autumn fog (nebbia) that blankets Piedmont’s hillsides at harvest, Nebbiolo is celebrated for its power, complexity, and extraordinary ageing potential. Key characteristics:

  • Flavours: Red cherry, dried rose, tar, leather, tobacco, liquorice, and earthy notes
  • Body: Full-bodied with high tannins and high acidity
  • Ageing potential: Exceptional — Barolo and Barbaresco can age for decades
  • Serving temperature: 18–20°C; always decant for at least 1–2 hours
  • Food pairings: Braised beef, lamb, venison, truffle dishes, aged cheeses, hearty pasta

Barolo vs Barbaresco: Italy’s Greatest Nebbiolo Wines

  • Barolo — the “King of Italian Wines”: the most powerful, tannic, and age-worthy expression. Aged at least 3 years (5 for Riserva). Key communes: Barolo, La Morra, Castiglione Fallètto, Serralunga d’Alba
  • Barbaresco — the “Queen of Italian Wines”: slightly more elegant and approachable. Aged at least 2 years (4 for Riserva). Key communes: Barbaresco, Neive, Treiso
  • Langhe Nebbiolo — the approachable entry point: lighter, earlier-drinking, and more affordable
  • Ghemme & Gattinara — northern Piedmont expressions: more rustic and mineral-driven

Serving & Decanting Nebbiolo

Nebbiolo’s high tannins demand patience. Always decant Barolo and Barbaresco for at least 1–2 hours before serving — or ideally longer for older vintages. Serve at 18–20°C in a large Burgundy-style glass to allow the wine’s complex aromas to fully open.

Prosecco Food Pairing & Serving Guide

Serving Prosecco at the ideal temperature is crucial to fully appreciate its delicate bubbles and vibrant flavors. The recommended serving temperature is between 665(266). Chilling Prosecco to this range helps maintain its crispness and refreshing acidity, while preventing the wine from becoming too cold, which can mute its aromatic profile.

Choosing the right glassware also enhances the tasting experience. Tulip-shaped flutes are traditionally favored for Prosecco as their narrow opening preserves the bubbles and concentrates the aromas towards the nose. However, white wine glasses with a slightly wider bowl can also be excellent, allowing more room for the wine to breathe and releasing a broader spectrum of aromas. The choice depends on whether you prefer to emphasize the effervescence or the aromatic complexity.

Food pairing with Prosecco varies according to its sweetness level:

  • Brut Prosecco: Its dry, crisp character pairs beautifully with oysters, sushi, and light salads, complementing fresh and delicate flavors.
  • Extra Dry Prosecco: Slightly sweeter, it works well with antipasti, soft cheeses like Brie or Camembert, and fresh fruit, balancing savory and sweet notes.
  • Dry and Demi-Sec Prosecco: These sweeter styles are ideal for spicier dishes, Asian cuisine, and desserts such as fruit tarts or panna cotta, where the sweetness harmonizes with bold or sweet flavors.

When opening a bottle of Prosecco, it is important to do so safely to preserve the bubbles and avoid accidents. Always chill the bottle first, then gently twist the bottle (not the cork) while holding the cork firmly. Slowly ease the cork out with controlled pressure to prevent the cork from popping abruptly and losing carbonation.

About Rioja

Rioja is Spain’s most celebrated wine region, producing predominantly red wines from the Tempranillo grape. Known for its distinctive oak ageing and elegant structure, Rioja ranges from vibrant and fruit-forward to deeply complex and age-worthy. Key characteristics:

  • Gran Reserva — aged at least 5 years (minimum 2 in oak); the most prestigious and age-worthy expression, produced only in exceptional vintages

Rioja Sub-Regions

  • Rioja Alavesa — Basque Country influence; structured, mineral-driven wines

About Tempranillo

Tempranillo is Spain’s most celebrated grape variety and the backbone of its greatest red wines. Versatile and food-friendly, it ranges from vibrant and fruit-forward to deeply complex and age-worthy. Key characteristics:

  • Flavours: Red cherry, plum, strawberry, leather, tobacco, vanilla, and spice

  • Food pairings: Lamb, roast meats, chorizo, Manchego cheese, paella, hearty stews, tapas

Tempranillo Regions

  • Rioja, Spain — the most famous expression; blended with Garnacha, aged in American oak with vanilla and coconut notes. Classified as Joven, Crianza, Reserva, and Gran Reserva
  • Ribera del Duero, Spain — known as Tinto Fino; typically 100% Tempranillo aged in French oak, producing more powerful, concentrated, and structured wines
  • Toro, Spain — known as Tinta de Toro; bold, rustic, and intensely concentrated from old vines
  • La Mancha & Valdépeñas, Spain — lighter, more approachable everyday styles
  • Portugal (Aragonez/Tinta Roriz) — used in Douro and Alentejo blends

Rioja vs Ribera del Duero

Both are Spain’s most prestigious Tempranillo appellations. Rioja is typically blended and aged in American oak — elegant, approachable, and vanilla-tinged. Ribera del Duero is typically 100% Tempranillo aged in French oak — more powerful, concentrated, and structured. Browse our red wine collection for both.

Origin and History of Tequila

Tequila, a distilled spirit that has taken centre stage in Mexico, has its origins rooted in the state of Jalisco. When Spanish conquistadors arrived in the 16th century, they found indigenous people making a drink from the blue agave plant. This tradition was soon adopted and refined to produce what we now recognise as tequila. Named after a small town in Jalisco, tequila is fermented and distilled in copper alembics, producing everything from un-aged blanco tequila to oak-aged reposado and añejo.

Types of Tequila

Blanco (silver) tequila is un-aged, allowing the natural flavours of the agave to shine through with citrus notes and a slight sweetness. Don Julio Blanco Silver Tequila is an exquisite example, offering a crisp agave flavour.

Reposado (“rested”) spends between two months and a year in oak casks, lending a golden hue and subtle oak spice. Casamigos Añejo Tequila is renowned for its smoothness and depth of flavour.

Añejo is aged for at least one year, resulting in a darker colour and richer flavours of dried fruit and vanilla. Patrón Anejo Aged Tequila offers a smooth sip with an enduring finish.

How to Enjoy Tequila

While tequila is often associated with lime and salt-laced shots, many tequilas are perfect for slow sipping. Reposado and añejo tequilas, with their notes of dried fruits, oak spice, and vanilla, are best savoured slowly. Tequila also takes centre stage in several cocktails — most famously the Margarita (tequila, lime juice, triple sec), as well as the Paloma and Tequila Sunrise. Understanding Champagne

Unique to the Champagne region of France, champagne is celebrated for its controlled production and distinguished effervescence achieved through secondary fermentation in the bottle. Its prestigious reputation is upheld through centuries of refined styles and strict regulations.

The History of Champagne

From its 17th-century origins in northeastern France, champagne has evolved into a global symbol of refinement and celebration. Historical influences — from the monasteries of Épernay to the grand houses of Reims — shaped the diverse styles we enjoy today.

Champagne Styles

Champagne varies by sweetness, aging, and grape types, each influencing its suitability for different occasions:

  • Brut — dry and versatile, ideal for a wide range of dishes
  • Extra Brut and Brut Nature — even drier, pairing well with delicate, lightly flavoured foods
  • Rosé Champagne — versatile with both light and richer dishes due to its subtle red fruit flavours
  • Blanc de Blancs — delicate and elegant, perfect with seafood
  • Blanc de Noirs — richer and more robust, ideal with meats
  • Demi-Sec and Doux — sweeter styles perfect for desserts or balancing spicy dishes

Vintage vs Non-Vintage Champagne

Non-Vintage (NV) champagne blends multiple harvests to ensure a consistent house style — ideal for everyday celebrations. Vintage champagne is produced only in exceptional years from a single harvest, offering greater complexity, depth, and aging potential.

The Champagne Aging Process

Aging champagne on the lees (spent yeast) develops greater complexity and richness, adding brioche, toasty, and nutty notes. Non-Vintage champagne is aged for a minimum of 15 months; Vintage champagne for a minimum of 3 years. Prestige cuvées like Dom Pérignon are aged for significantly longer.

Serving and Storing Champagne

Serve champagne chilled to 8–10°C in a tall flute or tulip glass to concentrate the aromas. Store bottles horizontally in a cool, dark place at a consistent temperature of 10–12°C. Non-Vintage champagne is best consumed within 3–5 years; Vintage champagne can be cellared for 10–20 years or more.

Champagne Food Pairing Guide

Champagne’s acidity and bubbles make it an exceptional companion to a wide range of foods:

  • Brut Champagne — oysters, lobster, smoked salmon, cured meats, fried chicken, aged cheeses
  • Extra Brut & Brut Nature — fresh oysters, sashimi, lightly seasoned dishes, caviar
  • Rosé Champagne — light poultry, salmon, charcuterie, strawberries
  • Blanc de Blancs — delicate seafood, fresh salads, goat’s cheese, sushi
  • Blanc de Noirs — roast chicken, duck, hearty meats, savoury vegetarian dishes
  • Demi-Sec & Doux — spicy cuisine, fruit tarts, crème brûlée, sweet desserts

Champagne Sweetness Scale

All champagne styles are defined by their dosage — the amount of sugar added after the second fermentation. From driest to sweetest:

  • Brut Nature / Zero Dosage — 0–3 g/L — bone dry, no added sugar
  • Extra Brut — 0–6 g/L — very dry
  • Brut — 0–12 g/L — dry; the most popular style
  • Extra Sec — 12–17 g/L — off-dry
  • Sec — 17–32 g/L — medium dry
  • Demi-Sec — 32–50 g/L — medium sweet
  • Doux — 50+ g/L — sweet; the sweetest style

The Main Types of Champagne

Brut Champagne

The most popular style worldwide. Dry, versatile, and food-friendly — Brut pairs beautifully with oysters, smoked salmon, cheese, and poultry. An excellent all-occasion champagne and the benchmark for most champagne houses.

Rosé Champagne

Made by blending a small amount of red wine into the base blend, rosé champagne offers a beautiful pink hue with aromas of red berries, citrus, and brioche. Perfect for romantic occasions, celebrations, and gifting. Pairs well with charcuterie, strawberries, and light meat dishes.

Extra Brut Champagne

With very low sugar content (0–6 g/L), Extra Brut offers a crisper, cleaner finish that lets the wine’s natural character shine. An excellent choice for connoisseurs and corporate champagne gifts for discerning clients.

Blanc de Blancs Champagne

Made exclusively from Chardonnay grapes, Blanc de Blancs is celebrated for its delicate elegance — citrus, green apple, chalk minerality, and a fine persistent mousse. Ideal for oysters, grilled lobster, and milestone celebrations.

Blanc de Noirs Champagne

A white champagne made from black-skinned grapes — Pinot Noir and/or Pinot Meunier. Richer, fuller-bodied, and more structured than Blanc de Blancs, with red fruit character. Ideal with hearty dishes, charcuterie, and caviar.

Sec Champagne

Slightly sweeter than Brut (17–32 g/L), Sec champagne has a gentle sweetness that pairs well with light desserts, fruit-based dishes, and mildly spiced cuisine.

Demi-Sec Champagne

A medium-sweet style (32–50 g/L) that is a classic companion for desserts — fruit tarts, crème brülée, and light pastries. Also a delightful end to a romantic meal.

Zero Dosage Champagne

No sugar added after the second fermentation. Zero Dosage offers pure, unaltered terroir expression — intense, precise, and mineral-driven. Favoured by connoisseurs who seek the most authentic expression of champagne.

Brut Nature Champagne

Essentially the same as Zero Dosage — bone dry with 0–3 g/L of residual sugar. Highlights the natural flavours and complexity of the wine without any sweetness. A thoughtful choice for the eco-conscious and the purist.

Doux Champagne

The sweetest style (50+ g/L), Doux is reserved for special toasts and rich dessert pairings — particularly decadent chocolate desserts and celebratory cakes.

Organic Champagne

Produced with a commitment to sustainability and natural processes, organic champagne is for those who value environmental responsibility alongside premium quality. An increasingly popular choice for thoughtful, conscious gifting.

What is Vintage Champagne?

Unlike non-vintage champagne, which blends wines from multiple years, vintage champagne is made exclusively from grapes harvested in a single exceptional year. Each bottle is a snapshot of that year’s growing season — its weather, its terroir, and the skill of the winemaker — making every vintage a unique and unrepeatable expression.

The Exceptional Quality of Vintage Champagne

In years blessed with warm weather, healthy grapes ripen to perfection, yielding wines of remarkable depth and elegance. As you sip a vintage champagne, you’re savouring the narrative of a specific year — the warmth of a sunny summer, the cool freshness of a crisp autumn, or the concentrated richness of a challenging harvest.

The Richness of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay

The primary grapes used in champagne — Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, and Chardonnay — flourish in the Champagne region’s unique climate. A warm, sunny growing season can result in even ripening and fully mature grapes, enhancing the richness and complexity of the final wine.

Celebrated Vintage Years

The 2008 Vintage

The 2008 vintage is widely celebrated as one of the finest in recent decades. A cool, sunny August led to even ripening and high acidity levels, producing champagnes of exceptional balance, brightness, and freshness.

The 2012 Vintage

The 2012 vintage stands as a testament to the resilience and skill of champagne producers. Despite a challenging growing season, the small yields produced wines of concentrated flavours and impressive structure. Also notable: Pol Roger Sir Winston Churchill.

The 2013 Vintage

Despite a tumultuous growing season, a dry, warm August allowed the grapes to ripen to perfection in 2013, yielding a harvest of balance and vibrancy. Dom Pérignon — which produces vintage champagnes only in years deemed exceptional — released a celebrated 2013 expression.

The 2015 Vintage

The warm summer of 2015 produced ripe, generous champagnes of great character. Highlights include the Moët Grand Vintage 2015 and the Pol Roger Brut Vintage.

The Artistry of Blending

Behind every great champagne is the artistry of blending — combining grape varieties, vineyards, and reserve wines to define the style and flavour profile of the final product. A remarkable example is Veuve Clicquot Extra Brut Extra Old, created from a selection of the finest reserve wines and an elegant expression of the house’s iconic style.

Whisky (or whiskey, depending on where it’s from) is distilled from grains, aged in barrels, and bottled at 40%+ ABV. But that's like saying pizza is dough with toppings – the magic is in the details.

  • Single Malt vs Blended – Single malt: One distillery, all barley (think artisanal). Blended: Mix from multiple distilleries (smooth & affordable).
  • Regions Matter – Scotland: Smoky Islay, fruity Speyside. Ireland: Smooth & triple-distilled. America: Sweet bourbon (corn-based).
  • Age Isn't Everything – A 12-year-old can be fantastic, but younger whiskies with great casks often surprise.
  • Proof / ABV – Higher proof (50%+) = more intensity. Start low (40–43%) for beginners.

Fun fact: "Whisky" is Scottish/Irish/Canadian spelling; "Whiskey" is American/Irish. But don't sweat it – the taste is what counts!

Step-by-Step: How to Taste Whisky Like a Pro

Grab a glass, pour 25–50ml (no ice yet), and follow these steps. It’s like a mini adventure for your senses.

  1. The Glass – Use a Glencairn or tulip-shaped glass (narrows aromas). Avoid rocks glasses for tasting – they let scents escape.
  2. Look – Tilt & swirl: Pale gold = young; deep amber = older/oak-aged. "Legs" (drips down the side) show body (slow = thick, fast = light).
  3. Nose – Sniff gently 2–3 times (don't inhale like a vacuum). Common aromas: vanilla (American oak), smoke (peat), fruit (sherry casks), spice (rye).
  4. Sip – Small sip, let it coat your tongue. Hold 5–10 seconds. Notes: Sweet (caramel), spicy (cinnamon), smoky (campfire), fruity (apple).
  5. Swallow & Finish – Note the aftertaste. Short & clean or long & warming? Add water if too strong – it opens hidden flavours.

Pro tip: Taste with friends – everyone's palate is different. One person's "smoky campfire" is another's "burnt toast". No wrong answers!

Whisky & Food Pairing: Don't Just Sip, Eat!

Whisky isn't just for rocks – it's a foodie's secret weapon.

  • Smoky Scotch → Smoked salmon, BBQ ribs, dark chocolate (smoke on smoke = magic)
  • Sweet Bourbon → Vanilla ice cream, caramel popcorn, grilled pork (sweet meets sweet)
  • Fruity Irish → Apple pie, mild cheeses, seafood (fruit cuts creaminess)
  • Spicy Rye → Spicy sausages, rye bread with cheese (spice amplifies spice)
  • Light Blended → Sushi, light appetizers (smoothness doesn't overpower)

Ultimate pairing hack: Dark chocolate + peaty Scotch = dessert for grown-ups. Try it – thank me later.

Common Beginner Mistakes (& How to Fix Them)

We all start somewhere – here's what not to do:

  • Mistake: Adding ice to everything – Chills flavours. Fix: Use large ice cubes or taste neat first.
  • Mistake: Gulping instead of sipping – Misses nuances. Fix: Small sips, hold on tongue 5–10 seconds.
  • Mistake: Ignoring water – High-proof can numb palate. Fix: Add 3–5 drops to open aromas.
  • Mistake: Sticking to one style – Boring! Fix: Try a tasting flight (we have sets).
  • Mistake: Overthinking – Whisky is fun. Fix: If you like it, that's all that matters!

Health note: Enjoy in moderation (1–2 drams max per tasting). Always with water & food to stay hydrated.
